name: Relative Valuation and Comparable Controls

positioning.oneLineSummary: Uses private and public comparables only after normalizing the multiple, time, fundamentals, lifecycle, and security rights.
positioning.productLabel: Relative Valuation Controls Lens — based on Aswath Damodaran's public multiples and VC-pricing materials
notAClaimOf: the latest financing round revealing intrinsic value
a preferred-share price applying to all common equity

attribution.display: Based on Aswath Damodaran's public multiples and venture-pricing materials

neutralParaphrase: Relative valuation is a pricing exercise that requires consistent multiple definitions, awareness of the distribution, identification of cash-flow, growth, and risk drivers, and selection of truly comparable firms or explicit controls for differences. Young private companies add lifecycle, survival, liquidity, stale-transaction, small-sample, and security-right complications.

locator.value: PDF pp. 4-17 and 21: four basic steps, definitional consistency, fundamentals, comparable selection, and difference controls
PDF pp. 11-12 and 56-64: young-company comparability, survival, claim rights, illiquidity, and relative valuation
VCs price businesses; four pricing methods; small samples, infrequent updating, opaque transactions, feedback loops, and lag

requiredConditions: The numerator and denominator belong to the same claim type, period, and accounting definition.
Comparable observations have transaction dates, currency, geography, stage, and source.
Differences in growth, margin, reinvestment, risk, survival, and lifecycle are controlled.
Preferred-security rights and dilution are normalized before extrapolating company equity value.

requiredEvidence.description: Verified company metric with period, accounting definition, currency, and normalization.
Versioned public or private observations with date, stage, geography, business model, metric, and transaction metadata.
Comparable differences in growth, margins, reinvestment, risk, survival, and lifecycle.
Preferred rights, option value, liquidation preference, dilution, and enterprise-to-equity bridge.

decisionQuestions: Is the multiple consistently defined and measured?
What is the current distribution rather than only the median?
Why are these companies or transactions economically comparable?
How stale, sparse, or selection-biased is the private sample?
What security rights prevent direct extrapolation from round price to total common equity?
positiveSignals: Metrics and claims are normalized before comparison.
The sample includes dates, dispersion, and transparent exclusion rules.
Fundamental differences are controlled rather than narrated away.
Public and private pricing methods produce explainable differences.
The terms service converts observed preferred prices to comparable economic claims.
redFlags: A median sector multiple is applied without dispersion or fundamentals.
Comparables are chosen because their valuations support the desired answer.
ARR, revenue, GMV, bookings, and run-rate metrics are mixed.
An old private round is treated as current market price.
Post-money headline value is applied to common stock without a waterfall.
disconfirmingEvidence: Comparable growth, margin, risk, or lifecycle differs materially.
Observed transactions are too stale or sparse for the current market.
Security rights explain much of the headline price.
The result reverses under reasonable comparable inclusion rules.
A fundamentals-based model cannot explain the selected multiple.
contraindications: Do not call relative valuation intrinsic value.
Do not mix enterprise-value and equity-value multiples.
Do not extrapolate a preferred round price without security normalization.
Do not hide sample size, date, and dispersion.

instructions: Define and normalize the target multiple.
Identify the fundamental drivers and control differences.
Normalize private security rights and time.
Report pricing separately from intrinsic value and send arithmetic to deterministic services.

sourceReliability.low: Valuations come from media reports without transaction or metric details.
sourceReliability.medium: Public filings and partial private metadata are available.
sourceReliability.high: Verified metrics, transaction documents, terms, dates, and public filings are available.

evidenceStrength.low: A single headline comparable drives the result.
evidenceStrength.medium: A distribution is available but important fundamental or term controls remain approximate.
evidenceStrength.high: A sufficiently broad, current sample is normalized and controlled.

evidenceCoverage.low: Only company name, sector, and headline valuation are present.
evidenceCoverage.medium: Metrics, dates, and fundamentals are covered but security terms or survival are incomplete.
evidenceCoverage.high: Definitions, distribution, fundamentals, lifecycle, survival, liquidity, terms, and timing are covered.

applicabilityConfidence.medium: A noisy sample exists with disclosed limitations.
applicabilityConfidence.high: Comparable claims and fundamentals can be normalized credibly.

judgmentConfidence.low: Only broad pricing context can be stated.
judgmentConfidence.medium: A pricing range is defensible with material caveats.
judgmentConfidence.high: The pricing range is robust across definitions, samples, and controls.

promotionRequirements: Validate metric and security normalization rules.
Backtest comparable selection and pricing ranges without cherry-picking.
empiricalQualifications: Private transaction samples are selected, sparse, stale, and often opaque.
Multiples reflect market mood as well as fundamentals.
A pricing range can lag a market regime change.

rights.notes: Public multiples and pricing principles are neutrally paraphrased.

openIssues: Define data licensing and private-transaction normalization requirements.
